newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - June 20.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - June 20.

text.p: The New York Times reported the following business stories Friday:
* The U.S. trade deficit grew 7.8 percent in April, drawing new attention to tensions with Japan and China as world leaders gather in Denver for a summit meeting.
* SBC Communications Inc said it expects to post one-time charges in the 1997 fiscal year of up to $2.3 billion in connection with its merger with Pacific Telesis Group.
* Unisys Corp Chairman and Chief Executive James Unruh said he is resigning from the struggling computer maker.
* The White House was growing edgy about the potential political ramifications as prospects of a tobacco settlement grow near.
* Northwest Airlines Corp has agreed to buy 50 A319 jets from Airbus Industrie. The deal is valued at $2 billion.

* David Bonderman, one of the principals of the Texas Pacific investment firm, is known for investing in businesses that have fallen on hard times but he believes are essentially good companies. He may now turn his sights to retailer Barney's Inc.

* A British judge has ruled that two penniless activists libeled McDonald's Corp when it said the fast-food giant had destroyed rain forests, discriminated against employees and poisoned its customers.
* The U.S. Supreme Court has ruled for the federal government in an 18-year dispute with Alaska over ownership of environmentally sensitive submerged lands rich in oil off the state's Arctic cost.
* The Dow Jones Industrials rose 58.35 points, closing at 7777.06, just five points off the record high.
* Television-industry negotiators broke off talks with parent advocacy groups seeking changes in the newly implemented television ratings.
* AT&T Corp named John Zeglis vice chairman of its board of directors, touching off speculation about the future leadership of the company.
* Merrill Lynch and Co Inc has agreed to pay $30 million to settle an investment by the Orange County district attorney into the county's 1994 bankruptcy.

* Procter & Gamble's Crest has long been the dominant toothpaste in the United States. But in the increasingly competitive world of making Americans' teeth sparkling white, Crest has seen its market share decaying.

* Market Place: One little-watched market indicator -- the ratio of stocks that advance to those that decline on the New York Stock Exchange -- suggests that stock prices may surge even further in the next year.
